name: THE COLBY BY YOUR NAME BURGER

recipe.history:
Colby cheese is one of the few genuinely American-born cheeses, developed in 1885 by Joseph F. Steinwand in Colby, Wisconsin — a small dairy town whose name the cheese now permanently bears. Steinwand, working at his father's cheese factory, modified the traditional cheddar-making process by washing the curds with cold water during production, which halted acidification and resulted in a softer, moister, milder, and more open-textured cheese than the sharp, dense cheddars being made around it. Wisconsin's dairy culture at the time was booming, built on the labor of German, Swiss, and Scandinavian immigrant farmers who brought with them deep cheesemaking traditions and found in the state's rolling pastureland conditions almost tailor-made for high-quality milk production. Colby quickly became popular because of its approachability: it melts beautifully, it's mild enough to appeal to broad tastes, and it carries a gentle, buttery, slightly sweet flavor that plays well with almost everything placed beside it. It became a staple of American deli counters, school lunches, and home refrigerators throughout the 20th century, often dismissed by food snobs as mundane precisely because it is so well-liked.

Colby's transition onto the American burger was almost inevitable given its melting properties and its ubiquity in the American dairy case. As diners and drive-ins multiplied in the postwar decades, cheese on a burger became an expectation rather than an upgrade, and Colby — along with American cheese — became a go-to for operations that wanted a reliable, fast-melting, crowd-pleasing result. Unlike aged cheddars that can break and turn greasy under heat, Colby's higher moisture content allows it to melt into a smooth, cohesive blanket over a patty within seconds, making it enormously practical in high-volume burger service. Food writers and chefs began to reclaim Colby's reputation in the 2000s and 2010s as part of a broader American regional cheese revival, pointing out that dismissing Colby as 'just' a mild cheese missed the point — its mildness is a kind of mastery, a calibrated restraint that makes it supremely useful. On a well-made burger with bold toppings, you want a cheese that harmonizes rather than competes, and Colby does exactly that.

I first took Colby cheese seriously at a roadside bar in central Wisconsin during a long solo road trip I took the summer after graduate school. I had been eating at ambitious restaurants the whole trip, chasing things that were interesting on paper. I walked into a place with a neon Pabst sign and a bartender who asked only 'what kind of cheese?' when I ordered a burger. I said Colby without thinking, and what arrived was a perfect cheeseburger — thick hand-formed patty, cheese fully melted and draped over the edges, pickles, yellow mustard, soft bun. I ate it at the bar and ordered another one. There was nothing to analyze or discuss. It was just one of the best things I had eaten on the entire trip, and the Colby was doing exactly the quiet, essential work it was built to do. I have never felt superior to Colby cheese since that afternoon.

Medium rare is the temperature at which a burger achieves its full potential, and this is not a debatable aesthetic position — it is thermodynamics applied to culinary logic. At 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, the proteins in the beef have begun to firm but have not yet undergone the full contraction that squeezes out moisture and flavor. The intramuscular fat is warm enough to be fluid and coat every fiber of the meat. The result is a patty that is juicy from its own rendered fat rather than from added sauces used to compensate for dryness. Colby cheese, with its cooperative melting behavior, rewards a properly cooked medium rare patty especially well: the cheese melts into the surface of the burger while the interior stays pink and warm, and together they create a bite that is simultaneously rich, savory, and gentle — a combination that requires no apology and no further embellishment.
ingredients: 1/2 cup warm mashed russet potato (1 medium potato, boiled and riced)
Kosher salt and cracked black pepper
6 oz Colby cheese, sliced 1/4 inch thick
1 tbsp dry white wine or water
instructions: 1. Make the potato buns: Dissolve yeast in warm potato water with 1 tsp sugar. Let sit 5–7 minutes until foamy.
2. Combine flour, remaining sugar, and salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with a dough hook. Add riced potato, eggs, warm milk, and yeast mixture. Mix on low until a shaggy dough forms.
3. Increase to medium and add softened butter in pieces. Knead 8–10 minutes until the dough is smooth, slightly tacky but not sticky.
4. Transfer to a buttered bowl, cover, and let rise in a warm spot 1–1.5 hours until doubled.
5. Punch dough down and divide into 6 portions. Shape into smooth balls and place on parchment-lined baking sheets. Cover and let proof 45–60 minutes until noticeably puffed.
6. Preheat oven to 375°F. Brush buns with egg wash. Bake 15–17 minutes until golden brown. Cool completely before slicing.

7. Make the caramelized onions: Heat butter and olive oil in a wide skillet over medium heat. Add onions and salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, for 35–45 minutes, reducing heat to medium-low once they begin to color. Add brown sugar and wine in the final 5 minutes. Onions should be deep amber and jammy. Set aside.
8. Make the yellow mustard aioli: Whisk together mayonnaise, yellow mustard, apple cider vinegar, honey, garlic powder, and salt until smooth. Refrigerate until needed.

9. Form patties: Gently combine ground chuck and ground short rib. Divide into 4 equal portions (~6 oz each). Form into patties about 3/4 inch thick with a thumb-pressed indent in the center. Season both sides with kosher salt and black pepper just before cooking.
10. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Cook patties 3 minutes undisturbed on the first side until a crust develops.

11. Flip patties. Immediately lay Colby cheese slices over each. Cook 2–2.5 minutes more. Pull patties at an internal temperature of 130–132°F. Rest loosely tented under foil for 3–4 minutes to reach 133–135°F.
12. Toast bun cut sides in butter on the griddle or in a pan until golden, 1–2 minutes.

13. Assemble: Spread yellow mustard aioli on both cut bun faces. Place a lettuce leaf on the bottom bun, then the rested, Colby-draped patty. Add a spoonful of caramelized onions and 2 pickle slices. Close with the top bun and serve immediately.
